PREFACE. 


VERY  single  record  which  tends  to 
throw  Hght  upon  the  Monastic  His- 
tory of  England,  illustrates,  at  the 
same  time,  in  almost  every  instance, 
the  civil  history  of  the  kingdom.  A 
collection  of  such  records,  the  care- 
fully-preserved Charters  and  Ac- 
count Rolls,  and  other  Documents,  of 
a  Religious  Establishment  from  its 
Foundation  to  its  Dissolution,  is  here 
presented  to  the  public,  abounding 
with  the  most  interesting  details  in 
illustration  of  the  Benedictine  In- 
stitute, of  the  history,  philology,  statistics,  manners,  and  cus- 
toms of  the  kingdom  at  large,  and  the  biography  of  individuals, 
and  claims,  with  a  concentrated  force,  the  attention  of  those  to 
whom  the  civil  and  religious  history  of  England  is  a  subject  of 
interest  or  inquiry.  These  records  are,  with  one  or  two  excep- 
tions, preserved  in  the  Treasury  of  the  Dean  and  Chapter  of 
Durham,   and   are   printed  by  their  kind  permission.*      The 

*  The  Charters  and  Indulgences  are  preserved  in  a  box  of  four  compart- 
ments, and  were  probably  removed  to  Durham  upon  the  Dissolution  of  the  Cell. 
An  endorsement  upon  the  back  of  each  proves  their  antient  arrangement.  The 
title  which  we  have  prefixed  to  each  is  copied  from  the  back  of  the  document, 
and  that  part  which  is  printed  within  brackets  is  in  a  later  hand.  The  same 
box  contains  several  monastic  leases,  which  we  have  not  noticed.  The  In- 
ventories and  Account  Rolls  are  in  a  box  by  themselves,  intitled  Finchale

In  the  latter  half  of  the  12tli  century,  certainly  after  the  year 
1 180,*  Henry  de  Puteacho,!  or  Pudsey,  having  become  possess- 
ed of  the  vills  of  Windegate  and  Essewell  (Wingate  and  Has- 
well),  near  Durham,  founded  a  monastery  at  the  latter  place, 
and  conferred  the  two  upon  persons  of  a  religious  order,  which, 
however,  is  not  named  ;  but  that  they  were  a  branch  from  the 
Church  of  Gisburne  or  Gisborough,  in  Yorkshire,  may  not  be 
doubted.  In  the  charter  of  a  subsequent  benefactor,  the  newly- 
founded  monastery  is  called  the  Church  of  St.  Mary  of  Hessa- 
well.  The  Charters  and  other  particulars  relative  to  these 
transactions,  with  the  previous  history  of  the  estates,  is  contain- 
ed in  the  first  seven  pages  of  that  part  of  this  volume  devoted 
to  Charters,  &c.  A  doubt,  however,  may  arise,  whether  the 
building  of  any  ecclesiastical  edifice  was  ever  actually  com- 
menced at  Haswelljt  as  we  almost  immediately  afterwards  find 
the  same,  and  other  more  extensive  possessions,  conferred  by 

*  See  Charter,  p.  4'. 

f  Henry  de  Puteacho,  Pusato,  &c.  for  his  name  is  written  in  various  ways,  was 
one  of  the  three  sons  of  Hugh  Pudsey,  who  was  Bishop  of  Durham  from  1153 
to  1196.  His  filiation  is  proved  by  Charter  li.  p.  46.  His  brothers  are  said 
to  have  been  Burchard,  Treasurer  of  the  Cathedral  of  York,  and  Archdeacon  of 
Durham,  and  Hugh,  Chancellor  to  Lewis  VII.  King  of  France,  who  died  in 
1189,  and  was  buried  in  the  Galilee  of  Durham  Cathedral.  The  mother  of 
Henry,  and  probably  of  the  other  two  also,  was  Adelis  de  Perci.  (V.  Dugd, 
Mon.  Angl.  New  Ed.  under  Sallay  Abbey.)  This  fact,  which  has  hitherto 
not  been  noticed,  seems  to  account  for  the  origin  of  Henry  Pudsey's  right  in 
the  parish  and  advowson  of  Giggleswic,  the  latter  of  which  he  conferred  upon 
his  church  of  Finchale.  Giggleswick  was  a  member  of  the  Percy  Fee  in  the  dis- 
trict of  Craven.  Henry  Pudsey  married  a  wife  of  the  name  of  Dionisia,  whom 
he  frequently  mentions  in  his  charters,  and  from  them  are  probably  descended 
the  Pudseys  of  Bolton  and  Barforth.  He  is  said  to  have  been  buried  at  Fin- 
chale. 

X  The  ruins,  near  Has  well,  are  apparently  those  of  a  chapel  of  small  dimen- 
sions, and  of  a  much  later  date.

Pudsey  and  other  donors  upon  a  newly-founded  monastery,  si- 
tuated in  a  warm  glen  upon  the  Brownie  streamlet,  at  a  place 
called  Baxtanford,*  (hod,  Baxter  wood,)  about  a  mile  from 
Durham,  Haswell  could  boast  of  no  such  natural  beauties  of 
wood  and  water,  and  this  was  probably  the  reason  why  it  was 
deserted.  This  second  monastery  was  also  dedicated  to  the 
Virgin ;  it  was  to  be  called  the  New  Place  upon  the  Brun  ; 
and  we  find  the  Canons  of  Gisburne  specifically  recognized  as 
the  Ecclesiastics  by  whom  it  was  to  be  peopled.  A  detachment 
from  that  Monastery,  under  the  superintendence  of  Stephen, 
one  of  its  dignitaries,  was  deputed  by  the  mother  church  for  the 
purpose.!  The  infant  establishment  met  with  other  benefac- 
tors in  addition  to  Pudsey,  their  chief  patron; J  but,  as  might 
naturally  have  been  expected  from  their  vicinity  to  the  rich 
and  firmly-seated  Church  of  Durham,  from  their  being  of  a 
different  order  from  that  establishment,  and  from  the  intermix- 
ture of  their  possessions,  harmony  did  not  long  prevail  between 
the  two.  Galfrid  of  Coldingham§  informs  us  of  the  various 
modes  by  which  the  Monks  of  Durham  harrassed  the  settlers, 
till  at  last,  as  he  says,  Pudsey,  sorry  for  what  he  had  done, 
begged  pardon  for  his  presumption,  and  an  agreement  was 
entered  into  that  he  should  abandon  the  Canons  of  Gis- 
burne, should  take  possession  of  the  Church  of  Finchale, 
should  confer  upon  it  the  possessions  previously  conceded  to 
Our  Lady  of  the  New  Place  upon  the    Brun,  should  stock  it

called  hake-stones.

of  severe  mortification  led  in  this  sequestered  spot,  which  he  tenanted  for  half

solitude.  He  died  in  1 170 ;  but  Bishop  Flambard  had  previously  granted

"  The  ruins  of  Finchale  Abbey  stand  in  deep  retirement 
three  miles  from  Durham,  on  the  southern*  brink  of  the  Wear, 
where  the  river  sweeps  over  a  rocky  channel  round  a  little  level 
plot  almost  covered  with  the  buildings.  The  woods  of  Cocken 
cover  the  wild  opposite  bank." 

We,  with  Mr.  Surtees,  leave  the  point  to  be  settled  whether 
this,  our  Finchale,  was  the  Finchale  rendered  famous  by  the 
two  Synods,  and  we  proceed  to  later  dates  and  matters  of 
greater  certainty. 

Th«  original  Finchale  t  stood  a  mile  above  the  present  Fin- 
chale, on  the  same  side  of  the  river,  and  became,  by  the  gift 
of  Bishop  Flambard,  the  residence  of  St.  Godric,  about  the 
year  1110.  Here  Godric  resided  for  a  while,  and  stubbed 
and  cultivated  the  plot  of  ground  assigned  to  him ;  but  by 
and  by  he  discovered  a  more  favourable  situation,^  "  planities 
non  modica,  situ  et  visu  ad  inhabitandum  accommoda,  ad  quam 
se  transferens  mansiunculam  veterem  deseruit,  et  oratorium  et 
domunculas  sibi  necessarias  construere  coepit."t  Here  we 
have  the  germ  of  the  present  Finchale.  Godric  soon  after- 
wards built  a  chapel,  which  he  dedicated  to  St.  John  the  Bap- 
tist, and  when  this  had  been  done.  Bishop  Flambard  granted  the

a  portion  of  land  beneath  higher  ground  by  the  side  of  a  river,  is  strictly  des- 
criptive of  either  Finchale.  But  what  is  Fink  ?  The  author  of  the  Life  of

The  documents  in  the  possession  of  the  Monks  relative  to  this 
estate,  which  came  into  their  possession  by  the  gift  of  Pudsey,

the  Oratory  of  Godric  and  his  successors,  but  as  their  revenues

other  accurate  information.**  In  1241,  the  building  of  a  new

fact,  tliat  Monastics,  in  erecting  their  edifices,  bad  other  aid  than 
that  of  their  own  resources,  or  the  casual  contributions  of 
visitors.  The  Archdeacon  of  Durham,  as  it  appears,*  com- 
manded his  clergy  to  admonish  and  persuade  their  flocks  on 
three  separate  Sundays  to  contribute  their  aid  to  the  fabric  of 
Finchale ;  and  as  an  inducement  he  tells  them  of  the  Indul- 
gences of  which  we  are  speaking ;  and,  moreover,  that  every 
contributor  to  the  building  of  Finchale  had,  and  would  for  ever 
have,  a  share  of  the  advantages  to  be  derived  from  the  religious 
services  of  the  mother  church  of  Durham  and  all  her  Cells. 
The  money  collected  was  to  be  paid  to  him  at  his  Visitation. 

It  must  be  understood  that  the  Monks  entirely  rebuilt  their 
church.  The  only  trace  of  their  former  edifice,  which  was 
suffered  to  remain,  was  the  tomb  of  Godric  their  patron  saint, 
which,  if  an  opinion  may  be  formed  from  the  portions  of  it 
which  were  discovered  during  the  late  proceedings  in  the 
church,  was  of  the  altar  shape,  with  Norman  pilaster  mould- 
ings at  its  corners.  These  are  the  only  stones  in  the  edifice 
which  bear  the  stamp  of  Norman  architecture. 

The  church,  such  portions  of  it  we  mean  as  have  not  been 
meddled  with  in  later  periods,  is  precisely  of  that  style  of  archi- 
tecture which  prevailed  during  the  period  of  the  Indulgences 
referring  to  it.  There  is,  however,  a  total  absence  of  ornament, 
save  that  the  western  door-way  has  some  good  mouldings,  and 
that  the  capitals  of  the  internal  pilasters  connected  with  the 
three  lancet-headed  windows  in  the  end  of  the  chancel,  the 
lavatory  near  the  high  altar,  and  the  capital  of  a  pillar  between 
the  chancel  and  its  northern  side  aisle,  have  been  tastefully 
decorated.     The  latter  has  a  profusion  of  ornament. 

The  annexed  ground  plan,t  with  a  few  brief  explanations, 
will  afford  a  correct  idea  of  the  extent  of  the  church,  as  it  was 
finished  in  126...,  of  the  alterations  which  were  afterwards 
made  in  it,  and  of  its  adjacent  buildings.  ABDDFGHH 
the  church.     A,  the  chancel.    B,  the  nave.    F  G,  the  transept.

PREFACE.  XIX 

D  D,  the  side  aisles  of  the  chancel.  H  H,  the  side  aisles  of 
the  nave,  C  and  E  were  subsequent  additions,  the  former 
perhaps  a  vestry,  and  the  latter  a  chantry.  The  central  tower 
was,  we  suspect,  no  part  of  the  original  church,  but  an  inser- 
tion, if  we  use  the  term,  during  the  Decorated  Period.  There 
are  indications  in  the  joinings  which  seem  to  warrant  this  sup- 
position. It  was  surmounted  by  a  low  and  heavy  spire  of 
stone,  which  was  standing  in  1655.  The  key-stone  of  the 
groining  of  the  tower,  ornamented  with  an  oak  branch  and 
acorns,  was  found  during  the  late  operations,  and  is  preserved 
in  the  adjoining  farm  house.  The  church,  however,  at  the 
Dissolution,  consisted  merely  of  A,  the  chancel,  B  the  nave, 
and  F  G  the  transept.  Long  before  this  period,  the  Monks 
had  totally  removed  the  aisles  D  D,  H  H,  and  the  buildings 
C  and  E  ;  converting  the  southern  aisle  H  into  the  northern 
alley  of  their  cloister  N.  The  arches  of  the  chancel  and  nave 
which  communicated  with  their  respective  side  aisles  were 
closed  with  masonry,  in  which  were  inserted  windows  of  the 
Decorated  Period,  one  of  which  is  remaining.*  Two  octagonal 
pillars  were  removed  from  the  south  side  of  the  nave  to  the 
farm-yard  K,  where  they  were  converted  into  three  supporters 
of  a  shed,  and  where  they  now  remain,  the  two  caps  being 
placed  downwards.  The  other  pillars  and  arches  were  inclosed 
in  the  new  masonry.  The  altar  (a)  in  the  south  transept  stands 
immediately  beneath  the  spacious  window  which,  as  has  been 
above  stated,  was  built  in  1266,  and  which  proves  its  age  by 
the  portions  of  its  tracery  which  remain.  In  front  of  this  altar 
was  the  shrine  of  Godric,  the  Norman  tomb  above-mentioned^ 
beneath  which  were  found,  in  1836,  the  bones  of  a  tall  man  bu- 
ried in  the  gravel,  apparently  without  a  coffin.  O,  an  open  pas- 
sage room  from  the  cloister  to  the  plot  of  ground  E,  which  was 

*  We  are  inclined  to  believe  that  these  alterations  were  commenced  in  the

Alter  these  architectural  digressions,  into  which  the  Indul- 
gences have  led  us,  we  return  to  the  concluding,  and,  in  our 
opinion,  the  most  important  part  of  the  volume  now  submitted 
to  the  Society. 

The  Account  Rolls  of  the  Priory  of  Finchale  subjoined  to 
the  Charters,  will  be  found  to  contain  materials  of  various 
kinds  for  illustrating  the  history  of  Finchale  itself,  of  the  order 
to  which  its  Monks  belonged,  and  of  the  customs  and  manners 
of  their  times,  but  most  especially  of  northern  statistics  and  phi- 
lology. They  owe  their  origin  to  an  Act  of  the  Convent  of 
Durham  in  the  year  1235,  of  which  we  give  a  copy.* 

Il.f  Quod  Priores  etiam  Cellarum  debeant  certificare  Priorem  Dunelmensem 
de  redditibus  Domorum  suarum  semel  in  anno.    /.  3. 

Item  statutum  est  per  eosdem  [the  Prior  and  his  Chapter]  ut  omnes  Priores 
Cellarum,  scilicet  Prior  de  Coldingham,  Prior  de  Insula,  Prior  de  Fynkall, 
Prior  de  Stanford,  Prior  de  Lithum,  Procurator  de  Jarue,  Procurator  de  Were- 
muth,  faciant  rotulari  singulis  annis  omnes  redditus,  possessiones,  et  omnia  pro- 
ficua  ad  ecclesiam  suam  pertinencia ;  et  unum  rotulum  tradant  Priori  Bunel- 
mensi  reservandum,  alium  secum  retinentes;  ut  in  fine  anni  possit  cognosci 
quantum  quselibet  ecclesia  creverit  singulis  annis  vel  diminuta  fuerit.  Item

anno  matricem  Ecclesiam  suam  de  Dunelmo,  ad  reddendam  rationem  de  statu 
Domorum  suarum,  ut  possit  cognosci  quantum  et  in  quibus  Cella  augmentata 
fuerit  vel  diminuta. 

Although  this  order  of  Chapter  was  doubtless  immediately 
obeyed,  yet  unfortunately  we  have  no  annual  report  of  the

until  the  period  of  the  Dissolution  the  chasms  in  its  returns  are 
numerous,  and  occasionally  of  long  duration.  That  such  an- 
nual returns  were  made,  however,  is  certain  ;  and  the  importance 
in  every  point  of  view  of  the  Rolls  which  have  been  preserved, 
will   excite  a  regret  that  the  series  is  not  complete.     Another

In  that  part  of  this  Book  occupied  by  the  Charters,  &c., 
will  be  found  several  documents  extracted  from  the  Registers 
of  the  Convent  of  Durham,  illustrative  of  the  government  of

by  the  Prior  and  Convent  of  Durham.f  The  Monks  of  Fin- 
chale were  Monks  of  Durham,  and  were  perpetually  migrating 
from  the  mother  church  to  one  or  other  of  her  Cells  and  back 
again,  or  from  Cell  to  Cell,  at  the  pleasure  of  the  Prior  of  Dur-

journed at  Finchale,  from  the  beginning  of  the  fifteenth  century 
to  the  Dissolution,  with  much  of  their  personal  history,  and 
minute  accounts  of  their  migrations  from  place  to  place,  but  w^e 
have  no  room  for  such  minuteness  of  detail.     The  number  of

XXIV  PREFACE. 

Monks  at  Finchale  seems  to  have  varied  from  time  to  time. 
In  1317,  there  were  nine.  A  very  interesting  document,  printed 
in  p.  30,  settles  them  in  1408  at  eight,  and  affords  some  valu- 
able information  on  the  subject  of  their  monastic  duties.  In 
the  middle  of  the  fourteenth  century  they  are  reproved  for 
keeping  a  pack  of  hounds  ;*  and  a  century  afterwards  they  had 
fallen  into  a  naughty  habit  of  wearing  linen  shirts  instead  of  the 
linsey-woolsey  of  their  order.t  At  p.  36,  is  a  proceeding  at 
which  the  men  of  Cocken  would  now  smile  ;  and  at  p.  29,  we 
have  a  direct  proof  of  one  advantage  at  least  resulting  from 
monastic  establishments — the  Prior  of  Finchale  feeds  and 
clothes  a  boy,  and  sends  him  to  Durham  School  for  six  or  for 
ten  years,  as  his  case  might  require.  The  letters  relative  to  the 
Rector  of  Houghton's  claim  of  tythe  coal  are  good  specimens 
of  the  English  of  their  period 4 

We  must  once  more  state  that  the  limits  within  which  we 
have  confined  ourselves  have  not  allowed  of  the  notices  and 
illustrations  which  might  have  been  given  in  almost  every  page 
of  the  volume,  especially  in  the  Account  Rolls,  which  contain 
a  mass  of  curious  information  respecting  the  fabric  of  the 
church  of  Finchale  and  the  persons  who  moved  within  its 
walls ;  and  the  most  valuable  matter  in  illustration  of  subjects  of 
a  more  general  nature.§ 

The  Glossary  and  Abstract  of  Prices  appended  to  the 
volume  will  be  found  not  devoid  of  interest.  They  may,  perhaps, 
pave  the  way  to  collections  of  the  same  nature  on  a  more  extend- 
ed scale.     Durham  affords  matter  for  two  large  volumes,  which

Prior  of  Durham's  camera  was  the 
present  Deanery.  The  Prior  of 
Finchale  had  a  camera  appropriated 
to  him  in  the  Infirmary  at  Dur- 
ham.

Cyrographatum,  112.  An  inden- 
ture in  the  proper  sense  of  the  term. 
Two  copies  of  the  deed  were  writ- 
ten on  the  same  parchment,  from 
the  middle  to  each  extremity.  Six 
or  eight  of  the  first  letters  of  the 
alphabet,  or  the  word  Cryrographa. 
turn  (from  y^np  and  y^cc^pa)  were 
written  in  large  characters  upon  a 
vacant  space  between  the  two,  and 
then  the  parchment  was  irregularly 
severed  with  a  knife,  as  a  check  is 
cut  from  a  banking  book.  As  long 
as  one  copy  remained,  the  forgery 
of  another  was  fruitless.

Plaerchambre,  ccxcviii ;    Player- 
CHAMBRE,  ccxcv.  A  chamber  in  the 
Priory    appropriated    to    dramatic 
representations,  such  as  the  Mys- 
teries, or  Miracle  plays  of  the  age; 
and  the  room  in  which  the  Monks 
assembled  to  hear  the  minstrels  and 
glee-men,  who  visited  them  for  their 
amusement.       Upon    one    antient 
dramatic     representation,    without 
doubt  performed  within  the  walls  of 
Finchale  in  its  day,  a  few  particu- 
lars may  be  here   recorded,  which 
will   probably    throw   a   new   light 
upon    the   history   of    Shakespear. 
Aubrey,  (Letters  from  the  Bodleian 
III.,  537,)  says,  that  the  father  of 
our  dramatist  was  a  butcher,  "  and 
I  have  been  told  heretofore  by  some 
of  the  neighbours,  that    when   he 
(Shakespear)  was  a  boy,  he  exercised 
his  father's  trade,  but  when  he  kill- 
ed a  calfe  he  would  do  it  in  high 
style,  and  make  a  speech."     Shake- 
spear's   father    may    have    been   a 
butcher,  for  any  thing  we  know  to 
the  contrary  ;  but  we  do  not  con- 
sider that  the  killing  of  calves  by  his 
son,  of  which  Aubrey  speaks,  is  to 


be  taken  as  a  proof  that  the  youth 
followed  his  father's  trade.  There 
was  an  old  dramatic  representation 
called  Killing  the  Calf.  The  per- 
former played  his  part  behind  a 
door  or  curtain,  and,  by  means  of 
ventriloquism,  acted  at  once  the 
butcher  and  the  animal.  The  one 
talked  and  pitied  ;  the  other  moaned 
and  seemed  to  pray  for  mercy,  till 
its  moving  solicitations  became 
fainter  and  fainter,  and  it  appeared 
to  die.  We  have  mislaid  our  refe- 
rence to  an  entry  in  a  lately  pub- 
lished miscellany',  in  which  a  sum  of 
money  is  stated  to  have  been  paid 
to  a  man  who  killed  a  calf  behind  a 
curtain,  for  the  amusement  of  the 
Princess  Mary,  the  daughter  of 
Henry  VIII,  before  her  accession 
to  the  throne,  and  therefore  long 
before  the  time  of  Shakespear;  and 
as  a  proof  that  the  amusement  was 
well  known  in  the  north  of  England 
in  modern  times,  we  give  the  fol- 
lowing extract  from  the  Newcastle 
Chronicle  of  2nd  December,  I775  : 
"  Lately  died  at  Barnard  Castle, 
Joney  Davie,  alias  Davidson,  aged 
95,  well  known  by  most  people  in 
the  county  of  Durham,  in  being 
noted  for  begging  about,  and  getting 
his  living  by  a  droll  performance 
which  he  called  killing  the  calf" 
The  son  of  this  man,  a  second  Joney 
Davie,  was  a  dancing  master,  and  he 
too  killed  the  calf.  H  e  died  at  a  very 
advanced  age,  about  t  venty  years 
ago,  and  was  buried  at  Stanwick,  in 
the  North  Riding  of  Yorkshire. 
And  now  comes  the  question — was 
this  the  calf  which  Shakespear  killed  ? 
and  was  his  mighty  mind  first  ex- 
cited by  his  popular  performance  of 
this  antient  representation  ?  Did 
the  applause  which,  in  his  boyhood, 
he  received  at  Stratford,  when  he 
killed  his  calf  in  high  style,  lead  to 
the  expanding  of  his  genius,  and  to 
that  immortal  name  which  he  has 
obtained  ?

at  Durham.  Many  of  them  were 
purchased  at  Ovingham,  on  the 
Tyne.  In  January,  a  "  seaym,"  or 
load,  of  fresh  salmon,  cost  9s.  The 
price  of  a  single  fish  varied  during 
the  season  from  Is.  2d.  to  6d.  The 
freight  of  eleven  barrels  of  salmon, 
from  Berwick  to  Newcastle,  cost,  in 
1531,  4s.  7d — Bursar's  Mem.

ccccxxvi.  After  all,  this  may  per- 
haps be  nothing  more  than  a  Deo- 
dand.  The  money  so  levied  was 
generally  paid  over  to  the  church,  as 
a  recompense  for  religious  services 
to  be  performed  for  the  soul  of  the 
deceased.

above,  p.  143.

lowing extract  from  the  AVill  of  John 
Casson,  of  West  Newbiggin,  dated 
6  June,  1580  : — "  To  my  said  son 
John  a  brasse  pot,  and  a  brasse  laver 
like  unto  a  horse,  being  heir  lumes 
upon  the  house."  This  may  have 
been  the  very  article  of  furniture 
previously  possessed  by  the  Monks 
of  Finchale.

RULES,  Sec, 

OF 

THE    SURTEES    SOCIETY, 

ESTABLISHED  IN  1834, 

In  honour  of  the  late  Robert  Surtees,  of  Mainsforth,  Esquire, 
the  Author  of  the  History  of  the  County  Palatine  of  Durham, 
and  in  accordance  with  his  pursuits  and  plans ;  having  for  its 
object  the  Publication  of  inedited  Manuscripts,  illustrative  of 
the  intellectual,  the  moral,  the  religious,  and  the  social  condi- 
tion of  those  parts  of  England  and  Scotland,  included  on  thfe 
East  between  the  Humber  and  the  Frith  of  Forth,  and  on  the 
West  between  the  Mersey  and  the  Clyde,  a  region  which  con- 
stituted the  Ancient  Kingdom  of  Northumberland. 

THE  SURTEES  SOCIETY 

I.  Shall  consist  of  an  unlimited  number  of  Members,  out  of  whom  shall  be 
iriennially  elected  a  President,  twelve  Vice-Presidents,*  two  Treasurers,  and  a 
Secretary ,f  who  shall  constitute  the  Council.  Of  this  number  five,  including 
the  Secretary  and  one  of  the  Treasurers,  shall  be  capable  of  acting  as  a  meeting. 
The  President  shall  be  ineligible  a  second  time  until  three  years  shall  have 
elapsed  from  his  departure  from  the  office.  The  other  Members  of  the  Council 
shall  be  capable  of  being  re-elected. 

II.  The  Officers  of  the  Society  shall  be  elected  at  each  Third  Annual  Meet- 
ing. Any  vacancy  which  may  occur  in  the  Offices  of  Treasurer  or  Secretary 
shall  be  provisionally  filled  up  by  the  Council. 

III.  Those  gentlemen  who  have  assented,  or  do  now  assent,  to  tlie  general 
principle  of  its  proposed  Rules  and  Regulations,  and  have  signified  their  wish  to 
become  Members,  shall  be  deemed  original  Members  of  the  Society.  In  the 
case  of  persons  applied  to  previously  to  the  27th  of  May,  by  Mr.  Raine,  at  the 
request  of  the  preliminary  Meeting  of  the  17th  of  April,  and  from  whom  no 
answer  has  been  received,  the  list  shall  be  left  open  till  the  first  of  July  next. 

*  The  number  ot  Vice-Presidents  was  increased  to  twenty-four  at  the  Anniversary 
in  1836. 

t  An  Under-Secretary  was  added  at  the  Anniversary  in  1836;  but  einoo  the  lamented 
decease  of  Mr.  Gordon,  In  1837,  no  new  appointment  has  be«a  made. 


2 

IV.  Subsequent  Members  shall  be  elected  by  Ballot  at  the  Anniversary;  eacfa 
jcandidate  having  been  proposed  by  a  Member,  in  a  letter,  post-paid,  addressed 
to  the  Secretaiy,  two  months  before  the  day  of  meeting.  The  Members  pre- 
sent at  tlie  Anniversary  shall  alone  be  entitled  to  vote.  One  black  ball  in  ten 
jshall  exclude. 

V.  Each  Member  shall  pay  to  the  Treasurers  an  Annual  Subscription  of  two 
guineas  in  advance.  The  sum  so  raised  shall  be  expended  in  transcribing  and 
publishing,  in  a  closely-printed  octavo  form,  such  inedited  Manuscripts  as  illus- 
trate the  intellectual,  the  moral,  the  religious,  and  the  social  condition  of  those 
parts  of  England  and  Scotland,  included  within  the  above  lines  of  demarcation, 
from  the  earliest  jjeriod  to  the  time  of  the  Restoration, — every  thing,  in  short, 
Avhich  has  a  tendenc}'  to  throw  light  upon  the  mind,  the  morals,  or  the  habits  of 
.our  ancestors.  No  apartments  shall  be  hired,  except  for  the  Annual  Meeting. 
No  collection  of  Books  or  of  any  other  nature  shall  be  formed.  The  Subscrip- 
tions, and  the  money  arising  from  the  sale  of  Books  under  a  subsequent  Kule, 
-shall  be  solely  devoted  to  the  transcribing  of  MSS.,  the  expenses  of  the  press, 
and  other  incidental  expenses 

VI.  The  Council  shall  itself  supply  matter  for  the  press  for  the  first  year. 
Afterwards  it  shall  annually  call  upon  twenty  Members,  in  alphabetical  order, 
for  notices  of  MSS.  which  they  who  are  applied  to  would  recommend  to  be 
printed.  These  notices  shall  be  sent  to  the  Secretary  within  a  prescribed  time, 
accompanied  by  the  manuscript  itself,  or  an  analyses  of  its  contents.  But  in  no 
instance  shall  any  Member  be  aj)})lied  to  by  the  Council  a  second  time  until 
«ach  Member  shall  have  had  an  opportunity  of  recommending  a  MS.  or  of  waiv- 
in.g  his  turn. 

VII.  No  MS.  shall  be  sent  to  the  press  by  the  Council,  without  the  sanction 
.of  a  majority  of  the  Members.  In  order  to  obtain  this  sanction,  the  Council 
shall,  by  their  Secretary,  transmit  to  each  Member,  upon  a  single  sheet,  a  con- 
xiensed  pnnted  account  of  the  various  analyses  which  have  been  submitted  for 
i:onsideration.  This  sheet  each  Member  shall  return  to  the  Secretary,  with  a 
jnark  in  the  margin  opposite  to  those  MSS.  of  which  he  approves  the  publica- 
tion. The  Council  may,  if  it  think  fit,  point  out,  as  a  matter  of  opinion,  such  in 
particular  as  it  approves.  The  votes  of  Members  who  return  no  answer,  shall 
be  at  the  disposal  of  the  Council.  When  there  is  a  deficiency  of  matter  in  any 
year,  that  deficiency  shall  be  supplied  by  the  Council. 

VIII.  The  expense  of  transcribing  for  the  press  every  M  S.  of  which  the  pub- 
lication is  determined  upon,  under  the  above  rules,  shall  be  defrayed  by  the 
Society,  if  the  Member  by  whom  it  is  proposed  should  require  it. 

IX.  No  matter  shall  be  printed  in  connection  with  any  MS.  save  what  is  ne- 
cessary for  its  illustration.  A  short  biographical  account  of  its  Author,  and  brief 
Kotes  illustrative  of  his  phraseology,  and  of  the  customs  and  manners  and  opi- 
nions of  his  time,  will  be  permitted  to  a  reasonable  extent,  with  the  modern 
names  of  the  places  which  he  mentions,  and  occasional  notices  of  persons  who 
occur  in  his  writings.  The  Council  shall  have  a  discretionary  power  of  reject- 
ing any  additions  of  the  contributor  which  do  not,  in  their  opinion,  come  within 
these  limitations. 

X-  The  nun.ber  of  copies  of  each  publication  shall  be  regulated  by  the  Coun- 
cil. Of  these  one  shall  be  given  to  each  Member,  whose  subscription  is  not  in 
an-ear.  The  rest,  of  which  the  Council  shall  in  each  case  determine  the  number, 
shall  be  sold  at  the  price  it  shall  appoint.  The  money  raised  by  sale  to  go  to  the 
general  fund. 

XI.  The  Armorial  Bearings  of  Mv.  Smtees,  and  some  other  characteristic 
xlecoration  connecting  the  Society  with  his  name,  shall  be  used  in  each  publica- 
jg,ion.     These  embellishments  shall  be  determined  upon  by  the  Council. 

XII.  The  selection  of  a  Frinttr  and  rublis'.ici  shall  be  left  to  the  Council. 


I 


XIII.  A  List  of  Officers  and  Members,  with  an  account  of  the  receipts,  ex- 
penses, and  general  proceedings  of  the  iSociety,  shall  be  annually  printed,  of  *n 
iiniform  size  with  its  publications,  and  transmitted  to  each  Member. 

XIV.  An  Anniversary  shall  be  held  in  Durham,  on  the  second  Tuesday  in 
July,  in  each  year,*  for  the  regulation  of  the  affairs  of  the  Society.  The  first 
Anniversary  to  be  held  on  the  second  Tuesday  in  July,  1835.  'The  Council 
shall  have  the  power  of  calling  extraordinary  Meetings. 

XV.  The  Society  shall  be  answerable  for  no  expenses  which  may  be  incurred 
at  the  Anniversary  Meetings,  save  the  hire  of  a  Room  for  the  transaction  of  its 
business. 

XVI.  No  alterations  shall  be  made  in  these  rules  except  at  an  Anniversary 
Meeting.  Three  months'  notice  of  the  alterations  proposed  shall  be  submitted 
ito  each  Member. 

*  The  Anniversary  was,  in  1836,  removed  to  the  foin-th  Thursday  in  September,

At  the  Third  Anniversary  of  the  Surtees  Society,  held 
at  the  Waterloo  Hotel,  Durham,  on  the  28th  of  September, 
1837, 

WILLIAM  LAWSON,  ESQ.  in  the  Chair;

Society  for  the  next  Three  Years. 

The  Vice-Presidents  of  the  Society  were  re-elected. 

The  Treasurers  and  Secretary  were  re-elected.

THE 

ANNUAL    REPORT 

OF  THE 

S  U  R  T  E  E  S     SOCIETY, 

FOR  THE  YEAR  1830-1837. 


The  Council  of  the  Surtees  Society,  to  whom  it  was  deputed, 
at  the  Anniversary  in  1837,  to  audit  the  accounts  and  to  report 
upon  the  proceedings  of  the  year  then  terminating,  present  the 
following  statements. 

The  list  of  Members  elected  at  the  Anniversary  in  1837? 
proves  that  the  objects  of  the  Society  continue  to  be  ap- 
preciated, and  furnishes  additional  means  for  prosecuting 
those  plans  to  which  it  is  devoted.  As  the  Members  of  the 
Society  increase,  subjects  to  engage  its  attention  appear  to 
increase  too.  The  enquiry  after  one  antient  author  has  brought 
others  to  light ;  and  unpublished  matter,  of  a  general  nature, 
but  of  the  highest  importance,  has  been  discovered  in  great 
abundance  illustrating  the  field  of  its  operations. 

With  respect  to  the  publications  of  the  present  year,  a  delay 
has  occurred,  the  causes  of  which  it  may  be  expedient  to  ex- 
plain. ^ 

The  Finchale  Records  were  found  to  be  more  numerous  than 
was  anticipated  ;  and  upon  examination  it  was  deemed  advisable 
to  print  the  whole  of  them.  Additional  time,  therefore,  was 
required  for  transcription  and  press  work.  Further  delay  was 
occasioned  by  the  engravings,  with  which  it  was  determined 


11 

that  the  volume  should  be  illustrated  ;  but  the  long  illness  and 
lamented  death  of  Mr.  Gordon,  to  whom,  in  his  official  capacity 
of  Under-Secretary,  the  editorship  of  both  the  volumes  was 
consigned,  have  been  the  principal  reason  for  the  tardiness  of 
their  publication.  This  editorial  responsibility  under  such  melan- 
choly circumstances  devolved  upon  the  Secretary  himself,  who 
was  already  deeply  engaged  in  other  pursuits ;  but  it  is  hoped, 
from  the  state  in  which  the  volumes  at  length  appear,  that  the 
complaint  of  delay,  if  any  has  been  made,  may  be  the  only 
complaint  to  be  made  by  the  Society.* 

In  any  Society  of  men  embodied  for  literary  or  other  pur- 
poses, however  numerous  the  yearly  accession  of  Members  may 
be,  the  names  of  many  annually  disappear  from  its  ranks. 
Some  withdraw  their  names.  Others  die.  It  is  the  custom  in 
many  literary  Societies  to  specify  the  names  of  the  latter  in  their 
annual  reports,  with  such  encomiums  as  they  may  seem  respec- 
tively to  deserve.  The  Surtees  Society  has  hitherto  contented 
itself  with  printing  in  black  letter  the  names  of  its  deceased 
Members.  In  the  present  Report,  the  Council  must  be  per- 
mitted to  depart  from  this  general  plan,  and  give  a  few  parti- 
culars of  a  gentleman  of  whose  valuable  assistance  it  has  been 
deprived. 

To  lighten  the  labours  of  the  Secretary,  who  had  gratuitously 
edited  for  the  Society,  Reginald,  and  the  Durham  Wills 
and  Inventories,  having  transcribed  the  greater  part  of  both 
these  volumes  with  his  own  hand,  without  cost  to  the  Society, 
Mr.  James  Gordon,  of  Richmond,  w^as,  after  due  notice  to  the 
Members,  in  conformity  with  the  XVIth  Rule,  elected  Sub- 
Secretary,  under  the  following  resolutions  of  Council : — 

Nov.  3,  1835.  Resolved, — That  the  Secretary  accept  the  ser- 
vices of  Mr.  Gordon,  as  his  assistant,  in  prosecuting  the  objects  of 
the   Society,  in  the  capacity  of  Sub -Secretary,  subject  to  the 

*  The  Preface  to  the  Sanctuaries  was  kindly  furnished  by  the  Rev.  Pro- 
fessor Chevallier,  one  of  the  Vice-Presidents  of  the  Society. 


approbation  of  the  next  general  meeting;  and  that  Mr.  Gordon, 
in  the  interim^  be  remunerated  in  the  san:e  manner  as  any  otlier 
person  or  persons  who  might  be  casually  or  permanently  em- 
ployed in  such  purposes. 

July  12,  1836.  General  Meeting. — It  was  ordered,  upon 
the  motion  of  Mr.  J.  G.  Nichols,  seconded  by  Mr.  Blackett,  that 
the  appointment  of  Mr.  Gordon  by  the  Council,  as  Sub-Secre- 
tary, be  confirmed. 

Mr.  Gordon  was  born  at  Gilling,  near  Richmond,  in  York- 
shire, in  the  year  1803,  of  respectable  parents.  He  received 
the  rudiments  of  his  education  at  Barnintrham,  under  Mr. 
Newby,  from  whose  tuition  he  was  removed  to  Ripon  School^ 
then,  and  still,  conducted  by  the  Rev.  W.  Plues;  and  afterwards, 
devoting  himself  to  the  law,  he  served  his  clerkship  to  an  at- 
torney at  Hull.  From  Hull  he  removed  in  due  time  for  a 
short  period  to  London,  and  afterwards  settled  as  a  solicitor  at 
Richmond,  in  Yorkshire.  Here  he  was  residing  at  the  forma- 
tion of  this  Society,  and  the  congeniality  of  its  objects  with  his 
favourite  pursuits,  led  him  almost  immediately  afterwards  to 
offer  his  services  to  the  Secretary,  to  whom  he  was  previously 
unknown,  in  conducting  through  the  press  any  work  in  which 
the  Society  might  be  engaged,  or  in  any  other  department  in 
the  range  of  its  objects  for  which  he  might  be  thought  compe- 
tent. This  oflPer  was  made  with  great  modesty,  and  it  was 
almost  immediately  accepted  under  the  above  resolutions.  Mr. 
Gordon,  in  consequence,  settled  in  Durham  in  the  end  of  the 
year  1835,  when  the  publication  of  the  Test  amenta  Ebora- 
CENSiA  and  the  Towneley  Mysteries  was  in  progress  j  but 
bis  health,  which  had  long  been  feeble,  had  so  far  declined  that 
he  was  barely  able  to  correct  the  press  of  the  two  volumes,  and 
compile  an  Index  for  the  former,  and  a  Glossary  for  the  latter. 
In  other  respects,  save  that  the  Preface  to  the  Towneley  Mys- 
teries was  (  bligingly  communicated  by  the  Rev.  Joseph  Hunter^ 
F.S.A.,  the  Author  of  the  Histories  of  South  Yorkshire,  Hal- 


13 

lamshire,  &c.,  &c.,  and  one  of  die  Vice-Presidents  of  the 
Society,  these  two  pubHcations  were  edited  gratuitously  by  the 
Secretary.  When  it  is  remembered,  that  the  Glossary  to 
the  Mysteries  was  the  work  of  an  invalid  labouring  daily  under 
the  most  dispiriting  ill-health,  and  compiled  during  the  short 
intervals  afforded  by  the  cessation  of  pain,  it  must  be  allowed 
to  evince  abundant  proof  of  what  might  have  been  expected 
by  the  Society  from  a  gentleman  with  whom  it  had  wisely 
connected  itself,  if  better  health  and  a  longer  life  had  been 
vouchsafed  to  him.  In  the  spring  of  the  year  1836,  Mr.  Gor- 
don's ill-health  seemed  to  be  rapidly  gaining  ground.  He  was 
low  in  stature,  with  a  spinal  mal-conformation,  of  a  slender 
frame  of  body,  and  of  the  most  feeble  digestive  powers.  To 
the  latter  he  had  systematically  attended  for  many  years,  totally 
abstaining  from  every  article  of  food  which  might  be  injurious 
to  him  ;  but,  notwithstanding  all  his  attention,  his  constitution 
at  this  period  appeared  to  be  visibly  on  the  decline.  His 
medical  advisers  recommended  a  change  of  air,  and,  in  conse- 
quence, in  the  month  of  June,  in  the  above  year  (1836),  he 
visited  a  relation  at  Caldwell,  near  Richmond,  purposing  to 
return  to  Durham,  and  attend  the  Anniversary  of  the  Society, 
which  in  that  year  was  held  in  July.  He  had  not,  however, 
been  long  at  Caldwell  before  he  became  confined  to  his  bed, 
and  in  this  bed  he  pined  away  for  ten  long  months  in  a  state  of 
the  most  extreme  bodily  weakness,  being  barely  able  to  speak 
in  a  whisper,  and  that  only  now  and  then,  but  patient  and 
resigned,  till,  on  the  4th  of  May,  1837,  in  the  34th  year  of  his 
age,  he  was  released  from  his  sufferings,  and  removed  to  another 
world,  for  which  he  had  from  his  boyhood  been  daily  preparing 
himself.  His  body  was  buried  by  the  side  of  his  father  and 
mother  in  the  church-yard  of  Gilling. 

Mr.  Gordon  had  from  an  early  age  devoted  himself  to  archai- 
ological  pursuits,  especially  those  of  a  philological  nature. 
In  the  dead  and  many  modern  languages  he  was  no  mean  pro- 
ficient ;  and  he  was  intimately  acquainted  with  the  history  of  his 


14 

own  tongue  and  its  various  changes  from  the  Saxon  period 
downwards,  and  had  made  the  civil  and  ecclesiastical  laws  and 
manners  of  his  country  his  peculiar  study.  If  Mr  Gordon  was 
learned,  he  was  modest  too.  His  natural  inclination  led  him  to 
shr^~  :c  From  genera]  society,  in  which,  as  a  literary  and  thinking 
ma  .,  i-'  found  not  much  of  gratification ;  and  his  general  feeble 
he*  ».ii  voufirmed  him  in  his  habits  of  seclusion.  By  those  who 
forUuiately  possessed  his  acquaintance,  his  highly-cultivated 
mind  and  his  modest  demeanour  will  be  long  remembered.* 

♦  Mr.  Gordon  greatly  assisted  Mr.  Frost  in  his  "  Notices  of  the  Early  History 
of  the  Town  and  Port  of  Hull."  He  was  the  Author  of  Robinson's  Guide  to 
Richmond,  1833 ;  of  a  Guide  to  Croft,  Dinsdale,  Darlington,  &c.  1834  ;  and  the 
compiler  of  a  Practical  Synopsis  of  the  Laws  relating  to  Bills  of  Exchange. 
He,  moreover,  contributed  a  few  occasional  papers  to  the  Gentleman's  Magazine, 
which,  it  is  believed,  are  generally  under  his  proper  signature.
